This weekend I went to dinner at Jupiter with two second-years I met that day. I had been to the restaurant before and ordered one small pizza. However, since I had skipped lunch and the two second-years ordered large pizzas, I thought: “I’m hungry, the large is not much more expensive - why not?”. 

After eating three slices (out of eight), I realized I was already full. The restaurant didn't have take-out boxes, so I couldn’t save the rest for later. That was the moment I realized I had spent more money than I needed. I forced myself to finish the pizza just because I had already paid for it.

Elasticity: how sensitive Q demanded is to P (at a specific portion of the demand curve
Slope of demand curve = derivative of demand curve (own price elasticity). Ƹ = derivative of demand x P/Q
Unit free (% change): change in Q (y) / change in P (x)
|Ƹ| > 1 → elastic (very) → change in P - large change in Q (luxury ou homogeneous goods) - when P > P*
|Ƹ| < 1 → inelastic (not very) → large change in P - Q almost same (necessities or unique products) - when P < P*
|Ƹ| = 0 → perfect inelastic (I) / |Ƹ| = 1 → unit elastic (E)
Shock in demand → increase in Q and P.
If supply is elastic (' more horizontal) = shock impacts more Q (long run curves)
LT → demand curves tend to be more flat/horizontal - more options/choice (for a given change in P, larger change in Q)

The conditions for segment pricing were present. First, there was heterogeneity in willingness to pay: startups faced budget constraints while corporations were open to paying higher fees. Second, we could identify “groups” using public information such as size, investments, and financial reports. Third, we could easily separate these segments in our pricing model, ensuring each one was charged appropriately.

The main threats are customer anger and competition. Some clients realized they were being charged different prices, which risked damaging trust. In addition, competitors could win projects by continuing to offer uniform rates to large corporations, which might force EZ to reconsider our pricing strategy. 

Still, segmentation expanded EZ’s client base and increased revenue overall.

As we learned with John Deree’s case, we shouldn’t include overhead costs (like Linkedin Recruiting license, rent, and salary of support staff) in the marginal cost. The right measure should then be the incremental hours that consultants and experts would spend on the work and other direct expenses, such as travel. However, estimating that cost was challenging, as we never knew how long it would take to find the right person for the position. There were also "hidden factors" like past training, accumulated experience, or prior similar projects that sometimes made consultants faster. And the opportunity cost of using a senior leader's time was hard to quantify, since we couldn’t predict future demand (project’s type, duration, price).
